extraction.body: Apple says well over 100,000 apps are now built for the iPhone Duo, a count it reached about two weeks after the foldable went on sale. The announcement is dated November 6, 2026, and it gives developers, buyers and rival phone makers their first hard marker for how fast the new form factor is filling out with software. The figure came from Apple itself, and CNET carried the statement from Susan Prescott, Apple’s vice president of Worldwide Developer Relations. She said, “Today there are well over 100,000 apps built for iPhone Duo already live on the App Store, and thousands of optimized apps are being added to the store each day.” That is the whole quantitative claim. Apple gave no exact count beyond the round number, and this analysis treats it that way. The milestone arrives while shoppers are still asking whether the device is worth waiting for. Our earlier report on iPhone Duo delivery quotes slipping to Jan. 22 covered the supply side. This piece covers the software side: what 100,000 optimized apps does and does not prove, which apps Apple named, and what the number means for the hardware race in foldables. Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. The timeline is short. Apple reportedly released the iPhone Duo on October 23, 2026, and the milestone statement followed on November 6. That is a 14-day window in which developers had to get hardware or simulators, rebuild against a new SDK, test two display configurations and push updates through App Review. Apple says more than 100,000 apps cleared that path, with thousands more arriving daily. Several outlets ran the same core fact on the same day. GSMArena, CNET, MacRumors, AppleInsider, 9to5Mac, MacStories and The Apple Post all reported the figure, and each tied it to Apple’s own wording. When that many independent newsrooms repeat one number on one afternoon, it usually means Apple distributed it directly. That matters for how you read it. The count is a company claim, delivered by the company, with no third-party audit attached. Still, the claim is specific enough to test over time. Apple says the apps are live, not announced, and that they target the iPhone Duo itself. Anyone with a device or an App Store account can spot-check named titles against that statement. The sections below do exactly that with the apps Apple listed. Separating confirmed facts from open questions is the first job in any milestone story. The table below lists what the reporting supports and what remains unstated. It is built only from Apple’s statement and the coverage that repeated it. Two gaps stand out. First, Apple gave no sales figure, so nobody can compute apps per owner or judge whether developers are chasing a large installed base. Second, the company gave no breakdown by category, so the 100,000 could skew toward small utilities or toward heavy productivity titles. Readers should hold both gaps open until more data appears. Reports say the counted apps were built with the iOS 27.1 SDK or later. That detail narrows the claim in a useful way. An app that merely runs on the iPhone Duo through compatibility scaling does not qualify. The number refers to apps that developers recompiled and adjusted for the new hardware, which is a higher bar than simple installability. MacRumors, whose report carried the headline “Here’s What’s Still Missing,” said it confirmed that the figure refers to apps built with that SDK. The headline itself signals that a gap remains between the 100,000 and the full catalog people expect on a flagship phone. MacRumors did not turn that gap into a number in the text we reviewed, and we do not guess one here. For engineers, the SDK gate has a practical effect. Reports on Apple’s developer guidance say standard SwiftUI and UIKit components adapt to both displays, so teams that already use those frameworks face a lighter lift than teams with custom layout engines. Apps with hard-coded screen assumptions need real work. That split likely explains why Apple can claim six figures within two weeks while still leaving visible holes. The iPhone Duo has two screens, and the reporting describes optimization as support for both. Apple’s wording, as relayed by outlets, says optimized apps use the full width of the inner and outer displays and place vertical controls in the status bar. That is a layout rule, not a cosmetic touch. It changes where buttons sit and how content flows when the device opens or closes. CNET described a 4:3 main screen and said Apple’s milestone shows developers adapting to it. A squarer canvas than a standard phone changes the design math. Lists can become two columns, editors can show a document beside a toolbar, and video apps can pick between letterboxing and reflowing their interface. Apps that simply stretch a phone layout look wrong on that shape, which is why the optimization label carries weight. The outer screen is the other half of the test. An app that looks good open but breaks when closed will draw complaints within days. Apple’s phrase about the full width of both displays tells us the counted apps handle both states. It does not tell us how well each app handles the transition mid-task, such as a video call that survives a fold or a draft that stays in place. Those behaviors will surface in app reviews over the coming weeks. Apple named a long list of optimized apps, and the grouping tells a story. Productivity and communication titles dominate, with a strong showing from Microsoft. Media, shopping, sports and AI assistants fill out the rest. The table sorts the named apps by category using only Apple’s list. That is 28 named titles out of a claimed 100,000-plus, so the list is a sample and not a census. Even so, the sample leans toward work and reading. Seven office tools and four notes apps suggest the early target audience uses a larger inner screen for documents, email and meetings. Streaming and sports apps point to a second use case, watching content on the squarer panel. Prescott’s remarks appear in several outlets, and they carry two messages. The first is the count. The second is tone. As 9to5Mac reported, she said, “It’s been wonderful to see how quickly developers have embraced iPhone Duo, and we’re grateful for their creativity and innovation.” That sentence frames the milestone as a developer success story, which suits Apple’s relationship with the people who build its platform. A second statement, reported by The Verge , looks forward. Prescott said, “The enthusiasm has been incredible, and we’re excited to see the pace of updates continue to accelerate as more and more apps optimize for iPhone Duo.” The phrase about accelerating updates sets an expectation that the daily additions will keep growing. Apple has now put that expectation on the record, which makes later slowdowns easier to spot. Both quotes come from a vice president whose job is developer relations, not sales. That role shapes the message. Developer relations teams want more apps, so they publish adoption numbers that encourage hesitant studios to join. A buyer reading the same statement should remember the audience. The point is to recruit developers, and it does that well. New form factors have always struggled with software. Early Android foldables, including Samsung’s first Galaxy Fold in 2019, shipped into an ecosystem where many apps did not know how to resize across a fold. Google later pushed large-screen guidance and launched its own Pixel Fold in 2023, and tablet-style layouts slowly became a normal expectation for Android developers. The lesson from that period is that hardware arrives first and software follows, sometimes by years. Apple faces a similar problem but holds a different set of tools. It controls the SDK, the review process and the storefront, and it can tell developers exactly which build version qualifies. The company also has a record of coaxing app support for new device classes, from the original iPad in 2010 to later screen-size changes on the iPhone. The 100,000 figure in two weeks fits that pattern of coordinated platform pushes. Two things set the iPhone Duo apart from earlier foldable launches. Apple appears to have asked developers to target the device before and during release, and it is counting only apps built with the newer SDK. A stricter definition makes the headline number harder to inflate. By contrast, older foldable ecosystems often cited compatible apps, a looser measure that included anything that merely launched. The strongest argument for Apple is consistency. A single SDK, a single store and one hardware family let the company roll out layout rules everywhere at once. The strongest argument against is scale. Android has years of large-screen experience across many makers, and its developers have spent that time learning to handle odd shapes. Apple compresses that learning curve into weeks, but compression is not the same as depth. For developers, the milestone redraws the cost-benefit math. A studio that skipped Android foldables might still adapt for the Duo because Apple customers tend to spend heavily on apps and because the company will likely feature early adopters. Teams with sibling iPad apps hold an edge, since iPad layouts already solve many of the same problems. Smaller teams without that code base need to budget for a few weeks of rework. For the wider hardware industry, the story sits inside a growing foldable segment. Mordor Intelligence’s forecast, which we covered when it projected foldable phones reaching $138.4B by 2032 , assumed that software support would improve as big platform owners joined. Apple’s entry and this early app push give that assumption some evidence, though one milestone does not validate a multi-year forecast. Component suppliers for hinges, flexible displays and thin glass stand to benefit only if consumer demand matches developer enthusiasm. Finally, watch your crash and review data after release. Fold transitions create edge cases that simulators miss, such as state loss during a posture change. Early reviews on the App Store will tell you quickly whether the update works. A fast follow-up patch costs little and protects ratings during the launch window when Apple’s featuring teams are paying attention. Several questions have no public answer today. Apple has not provided an exact app total, a split by category or a count of how many of the 100,000 are new apps versus updates to existing ones. It has not shared iPhone Duo pricing in the milestone statement, nor sales, specifications beyond what outlets described, or a roadmap for further SDK changes. Anyone presenting those details as settled is going beyond the record. The quality of optimization is also unmeasured. A count of apps built for the Duo tells us they target the device. It does not tell us how many use both displays well, how many ship with bugs or how many just meet the minimum. Independent testers will fill that gap over time. Until they do, treat the 100,000 as a measure of effort and not of polish. The Duo is not the only Apple device drawing developer attention this year. Rumors about the next Pro iPhone, including the under-display Face ID reports for the iPhone 18 Pro , show Apple working on several screen changes at once. Each change asks developers to revisit layouts, and a smooth Duo rollout makes the next one easier to sell. The company also gains a testing ground. Lessons from the Duo’s two-display behavior can inform future products, and developers who now understand posture-aware layouts will carry that skill forward. In that sense, the 100,000 figure is less about one phone and more about training an entire developer base for what comes next. Hardware cycles run for years, and software habits stick. How many apps are optimized for iPhone Duo? Apple says well over 100,000 apps are built for the device and live on the App Store. It gave no exact total, and outlets reporting the news repeated that wording. When did the iPhone Duo launch? Reports give October 23, 2026 as the launch date. Apple’s milestone statement is dated November 6, 2026, two weeks later. Which apps are already optimized? Apple named Microsoft Word, Excel, PowerPoint and Outlook, Zoom, Etsy, Halide Mark III, Spotify, CBS, Tubi, BBC iPlayer (UK), Apple Music Classical, NBA, NHL, Yahoo Fantasy Sports, Sportsnet (Canada), Facebook Messenger, Google Chat, ChatGPT, Grok Bot, Microsoft Copilot, SAP Concur, monday.com, Extra, Goodnotes, PDF Expert, Documents and iA Writer. What does optimized mean in practice? According to reports, optimized apps support the full width of the inner and outer displays and place vertical controls in the status bar. CNET described the main screen as 4:3. Does the milestone show how well the iPhone Duo is selling? No. Apple did not disclose sales, price or detailed specifications in the statement, so the app count cannot stand in for demand.

Apple gave no exact count beyond the round number, and this analysis treats it that way.
The announcement is dated November 6, 2026, and it gives developers, buyers and rival phone makers their first hard marker for how fast the new form factor is filling out with software.
The milestone arrives while shoppers are still asking whether the device is worth waiting for.
Our earlier report on iPhone Duo delivery quotes slipping to Jan.
That is a 14-day window in which developers had to get hardware or simulators, rebuild against a new SDK, test two display configurations and push updates through App Review.
Apple faces a similar problem but holds a different set of tools.
It controls the SDK, the review process and the storefront, and it can tell developers exactly which build version qualifies.
The company also has a record of coaxing app support for new device classes, from the original iPad in 2010 to later screen-size changes on the iPhone.
The 100,000 figure in two weeks fits that pattern of coordinated platform pushes.
Several questions have no public answer today.
It has not shared iPhone Duo pricing in the milestone statement, nor sales, specifications beyond what outlets described, or a roadmap for further SDK changes.
Anyone presenting those details as settled is going beyond the record.
MacRumors did not turn that gap into a number in the text we reviewed, and we do not guess one here.
According to reports, optimized apps support the full width of the inner and outer displays and place vertical controls in the status bar.
Readers should hold both gaps open until more data appears.
Even so, the sample leans toward work and reading.
Seven office tools and four notes apps suggest the early target audience uses a larger inner screen for documents, email and meetings.
Streaming and sports apps point to a second use case, watching content on the squarer panel.
The sections below do exactly that with the apps Apple listed.
Apple appears to have asked developers to target the device before and during release, and it is counting only apps built with the newer SDK.
The quality of optimization is also unmeasured.
It does not tell us how many use both displays well, how many ship with bugs or how many just meet the minimum.
Independent testers will fill that gap over time.
Lessons from the Duo’s two-display behavior can inform future products, and developers who now understand posture-aware layouts will carry that skill forward.
Hardware cycles run for years, and software habits stick.
A studio that skipped Android foldables might still adapt for the Duo because Apple customers tend to spend heavily on apps and because the company will likely feature early adopters.
Rumors about the next Pro iPhone, including the under-display Face ID reports for the iPhone 18 Pro , show Apple working on several screen changes at once.

extraction.body: Apple today announced that more than 100,000 apps have been optimized for the iPhone Duo, released two weeks ago. We confirmed that this figure refers to apps built with the iOS 27.1 SDK or later , meaning these apps fill the full width of the iPhone Duo's inner and outer displays and have vertical controls in the status bar. A statement from Susan Prescott, Apple's Vice President of Worldwide Developer Relations: It's been wonderful to see how quickly developers have embraced iPhone Duo, and we're grateful for their creativity and innovation. Today there are well over 100,000 apps built for iPhone Duo already live on the App Store, and thousands of optimized apps are being added to the store each day. In the last month alone, thousands of developers have joined us for workshops in 19 cities around the world to experience iPhone Duo firsthand and bring updated apps to their users. The enthusiasm has been incredible, and we're excited to see the pace of updates continue to accelerate as more and more apps optimize for iPhone Duo. Apple said thousands of apps optimized for the iPhone Duo are being added to the App Store each day, with recent examples including Microsoft's Excel, OneNote, PowerPoint, and Word apps , along with the Etsy, Goodnotes, Halide Mark III, NBA, NHL, and Zoom apps. Other apps optimized for the device include Amazon Prime Video, Fantastical, Flighty, Instagram, MLB, Netflix, SmartGym, WhatsApp, YouTube, and more. There are too many to list. Apps optimized for the iPhone Duo have a "Made for iPhone Duo" badge in their App Store listings on the device, making them easy to identify. iOS 27.2 added Apple Pencil (USB-C) support to the iPhone Duo , enabling users to draw in apps like Procreate Pocket, take notes in Apple Notes, Fineliner, and TypeDraw, and mark up documents in apps like Preview on the device. On the other hand, with millions of apps available in the App Store, there are unsurprisingly many apps that are still not optimized for the iPhone Duo, with the following examples listed in alphabetical order: AMC Theaters, Amazon Fire TV, Apple Store, Best Buy, Bluesky, Delta, DoorDash, Duolingo, Fandango, FedEx, Goodreads, Google Docs, Google Home, Google Sheets, Google Slides, GrubHub, JetBlue, Libby, Microsoft Authenticator, Microsoft Teams, MTA, Nike, PayPal, PictureThis, Ring, Southwest, Spectrum TV, Starbucks, Steam, Uber Eats, UPS, USPS, Venmo, Verizon, Wells Fargo, Whole Foods, and YouTube Music. Apple said developers can easily optimize their apps for the iPhone Duo. Apps that use standard SwiftUI and UIKit components adapt automatically to each display, with controls moved to the status bar and multi-column support on the inner display. New APIs let developers optimize their apps for the device's various layouts and poses. Apple has hosted more than 50 in-person iPhone Duo app workshops in 19 cities worldwide, and there are online resources like the Apple Developer Forums . In the meantime, apps built with the iOS 27 SDK resize to fill most of the inner display on the iPhone Duo, but they avoid the status bar on the right edge. Apps built with the iOS 26 SDK or earlier run on the iPhone Duo, but appear in the center of the inner display, with lots of empty black space on the left and right sides of the apps. iPhone Duo app optimization has been a hotly debated topic on social media platforms, with some people pointing out apps that are not yet optimized and others saying the issue is overblown. It is clearly a mixed bag, with some apps optimized and some not. More apps are being updated by the day, though, so the situation is improving rapidly. New features and lesser-known changes to check out if you're upgrading. Siri AI improvements, Suggestions in Messages, Apple Music rebrand, and more. Apple's iPhone Duo is in customers' hands, and our dedicated how-to series explains the new features worth trying first. Spec bump to the M6 chip for the low-end 14-inch model, plus new high-end PROLED XDR models with touchscreen displays. 8.5-inch OLED display, A20 Pro chip, IP67 water and dust resistance, and a thinner and lighter design. Apple's smart home hub with 7-inch square display, A18 chip with Siri AI support, and more. sources.title: Heightened security, gameday changes set for LSU-Alabama game ahead of Melania Trump's visit - WBRZ
passages: BATON ROUGE — LSU Athletics has issued an urgent advisory alerting fans to heightened security measures, road closures and stadium entry adjustments ahead of Saturday's matchup against Alabama at Tiger Stadium.

The elevated security protocols follow the announcement that First Lady Melania Trump will attend the rivalry game to present a $5 million gift from an LSU Foundation donor, establishing a permanent endowed scholarship for her Fostering the Future initiative.

Due to security perimeters and access route restrictions around the stadium, LSU has updated entry points for suite holders and fans requiring accessible routing: Gates 11–12 and Gates 22–28 will scan suite tickets for patrons requiring ADA or alternative accessible pathways.

The elevated security protocols follow the announcement that First Lady Melania Trump will attend the rivalry game to present a $5 million gift from an LSU Foundation donor, establishing a permanent endowed scholarship for her Fostering the Future initiative. Working alongside the U.S. Secret Service and local law enforcement, LSU officials are urging ticket holders to prepare for widespread campus delays and extended screening times. Interior campus streets will begin shutting down at 5 a.m. Saturday. Stadium gates open at 9 a.m. Fans are advised to arrive significantly earlier than usual to clear security checkpoints. Strict screening measures will be enforced at all stadium entrances. Attendees should review the official prohibited items list before approaching the gates to prevent entrance delays. Prohibited items include aerosols, bicycles, coolers, drones, laser pointers, pepper spray, selfie sticks, toy guns, weapons, etc. Due to security perimeters and access route restrictions around the stadium, LSU has updated entry points for suite holders and fans requiring accessible routing: Gates 11–12 and Gates 22–28 will scan suite tickets for patrons requiring ADA or alternative accessible pathways. Once inside, fans heading to the suites should proceed east/southeast toward Gates 20–21 to reach the suite elevators. Fans encountering issues on campus or inside the stadium can text "LSU" plus their issue and location to 69050. The area surrounding LSU's Chemical Engineering Building and Power House will be restricted to the public. Fans can use the designated walkway from South Stadium Drive to Field House Drive.

extraction.body: BATON ROUGE, La. (WAFB) - Fans heading to Saturday’s LSU-Alabama game should expect increased security, campus closures, and possible delays as First Lady Melania Trump visits Tiger Stadium, LSU Athletics said in an email to ticket holders. The First Lady is scheduled to attend the game and announce a $5 million gift from an LSU Foundation donor to establish a Fostering the Future endowed scholarship, according to the email. LSU said the changes are tied to the visit and on-site operations with the U.S. Secret Service. The university cautioned that the guidelines and impacts are at the Secret Service’s discretion and could change throughout the day. LSU is urging fans to allow extra time for parking, navigating campus, and getting to their seats. The university said visitors should expect campuswide delays, disruptions, and heightened security checkpoints. Increased security will be in place throughout the stadium, and screening will be mandatory for all patrons, regardless of their credentials, according to the email. Additional security protocols will also be in place in stadium clubs and suites. LSU said fans will be able to reach their ticketed seats, but access to some areas within premium spaces will be restricted, potentially causing delays. LSU said the area marked in red on its game day map will be completely closed. Parking, driving, walking, and tailgating will not be allowed there, and tailgates normally located in the restricted footprint must relocate for the day. No credential, including an all-access credential, will permit entry into the restricted area, LSU said. Yellow outlines on the map show open pedestrian routes around the closures. For suite ticket holders who need an accessible route and cannot reach their usual entrance because of campus closures, LSU said Gates 11-12 and 22-28 have been updated to scan suite tickets. Once inside, those patrons should proceed east or southeast toward Gates 20-21 to reach the suite elevators, according to the email. LSU also urged fans to review the prohibited-items graphic included in its game day information before approaching the gates.

Due to security perimeters and access route restrictions around the stadium, LSU has updated entry points for suite holders and fans requiring accessible routing: Gates 11–12 and Gates 22–28 will scan suite tickets for patrons requiring ADA or alternative accessible pathways.

Additional security protocols will also be in place in stadium clubs and suites.
LSU said fans will be able to reach their ticketed seats, but access to some areas within premium spaces will be restricted, potentially causing delays.
LSU said the changes are tied to the visit and on-site operations with the U.S.

extraction.body: BATON ROUGE — LSU Athletics has issued an urgent advisory alerting fans to heightened security measures, road closures and stadium entry adjustments ahead of Saturday's matchup against Alabama at Tiger Stadium. The elevated security protocols follow the announcement that First Lady Melania Trump will attend the rivalry game to present a $5 million gift from an LSU Foundation donor, establishing a permanent endowed scholarship for her Fostering the Future initiative. Working alongside the U.S. Secret Service and local law enforcement, LSU officials are urging ticket holders to prepare for widespread campus delays and extended screening times. Interior campus streets will begin shutting down at 5 a.m. Saturday. Stadium gates open at 9 a.m. Fans are advised to arrive significantly earlier than usual to clear security checkpoints. Strict screening measures will be enforced at all stadium entrances. Attendees should review the official prohibited items list before approaching the gates to prevent entrance delays. Prohibited items include aerosols, bicycles, coolers, drones, laser pointers, pepper spray, selfie sticks, toy guns, weapons, etc. Due to security perimeters and access route restrictions around the stadium, LSU has updated entry points for suite holders and fans requiring accessible routing: Gates 11–12 and Gates 22–28 will scan suite tickets for patrons requiring ADA or alternative accessible pathways. Once inside, fans heading to the suites should proceed east/southeast toward Gates 20–21 to reach the suite elevators. Fans encountering issues on campus or inside the stadium can text "LSU" plus their issue and location to 69050. The area surrounding LSU's Chemical Engineering Building and Power House will be restricted to the public. Fans can use the designated walkway from South Stadium Drive to Field House Drive.

extraction.body: BATON ROUGE, La. (WAFB) - Fans heading to Saturday’s LSU-Alabama game should expect increased security, campus closures, and possible delays as First Lady Melania Trump visits Tiger Stadium, LSU Athletics said in an email to ticket holders. The First Lady is scheduled to attend the game and announce a $5 million gift from an LSU Foundation donor to establish a Fostering the Future endowed scholarship, according to the email. LSU said the changes are tied to the visit and on-site operations with the U.S. Secret Service. The university cautioned that the guidelines and impacts are at the Secret Service’s discretion and could change throughout the day. LSU is urging fans to allow extra time for parking, navigating campus, and getting to their seats. The university said visitors should expect campuswide delays, disruptions, and heightened security checkpoints. Increased security will be in place throughout the stadium, and screening will be mandatory for all patrons, regardless of their credentials, according to the email. Additional security protocols will also be in place in stadium clubs and suites. LSU said fans will be able to reach their ticketed seats, but access to some areas within premium spaces will be restricted, potentially causing delays. LSU said the area marked in red on its game day map will be completely closed. Parking, driving, walking, and tailgating will not be allowed there, and tailgates normally located in the restricted footprint must relocate for the day. No credential, including an all-access credential, will permit entry into the restricted area, LSU said. Yellow outlines on the map show open pedestrian routes around the closures. For suite ticket holders who need an accessible route and cannot reach their usual entrance because of campus closures, LSU said Gates 11-12 and 22-28 have been updated to scan suite tickets. Once inside, those patrons should proceed east or southeast toward Gates 20-21 to reach the suite elevators, according to the email. LSU also urged fans to review the prohibited-items graphic included in its game day information before approaching the gates.

Wall Street appears to have found a silver lining following the Democrats' sweeping victories in the 2026 midterm elections. With Democrats gaining control of both chambers of Congress , investors are considering whether more regulation could slow the construction of artificial intelligence (AI) data centers across the United States. At first glance, that might actually benefit Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT), Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN), Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOGL) (NASDAQ: GOOG), and Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META). After all, building AI infrastructure is expensive. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » If Big Tech is forced to reduce capital expenditures (capex), their free cash flow could improve. Meanwhile, a shortage of compute capacity could allow existing data center operators to charge higher prices. While this all makes sense in theory, I think Wall Street may be overlooking an important possibility. Over the last several years, the hyperscalers have committed hundreds of billions of dollars to expanding AI infrastructure. These investments include procuring graphics processing units (GPUs), building data centers, and securing electricity. However, a number of candidates used data centers as a controversial topic during their time on the campaign trail. For many people around the country, data centers have fueled rising utility costs. Following the midterms, Wall Street is considering whether new legislation or tighter permitting requirements could make additional U.S. data center projects more difficult to pursue. The financial argument is pretty straightforward: If the hyperscalers slow down their infrastructure investments, capex would decline and free cash flow would rise. At the same time, continued demand for compute could create a supply demand imbalance. Companies with existing capacity would be in a position to charge higher utilization and command pricing power. The combination of lower spending and higher revenue per unit of compute would be favorable for the hyperscalers. With that said, this assumes that AI developers respond to potential regulatory restrictions by slowing down the pace of their infrastructure roadmaps. During a discussion with The Wall Street Journal on Nov. 4, Meta's president and vice chair, Dina Powell McCormick, acknowledged that the election results could complicate future data center development domestically. She says starting new domestic projects may be harder and raised a question that could reshape the AI investment narrative: "Do we need to build outside the United States?" There's already evidence that Big Tech is willing to invest internationally. Consider some of their existing projects: More than $10 billion is planned across the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Kuwait through 2030. More than $5 billion is planned in Mexico over 15 years. A $15 billion AI infrastructure investment planned for Visakhapatnam, India between 2026 and 2030. 13 billion Canadian dollars for a 1-gigawatt AI data center in Alberta, plus a 168-megawatt AI data center lease agreement in Jamnagar, India. Data source: Company press releases, Wall Street Journal , Reuters. These investments were announced before the midterms, so they shouldn't be interpreted as reactions to the election. Nevertheless, they demonstrate that hyperscalers already have international infrastructure strategies in place. If new restrictions make projects in certain states less attractive, I wouldn't be surprised to see Big Tech evaluate opportunities elsewhere and accelerate overseas development. Suppose new federal or state regulations delay data center construction in the U.S. Initially, the hyperscalers may postpone their projects, causing capex to decline and free cash flow to improve. In turn, investors may cheer these tighter cost controls and higher profits, leading to rising stock prices. Still, I question whether the hyperscalers would willingly delay expansion plans for two years while waiting for the 2028 presidential election. That strategy introduces another layer of uncertainty without guaranteeing a more favorable regulatory environment afterward. Most importantly, redirecting AI infrastructure investments overseas would not generate the sustained improvements to cash flow Wall Street is anticipating. The hyperscalers could easily continue pouring hundreds of billions of dollars annually on AI infrastructure, just in different countries. Ultimately, I think investors need to distinguish between a slowdown in U.S. data center construction and a slowdown in global AI investment. Those are two different outcomes. For now, Wall Street seems interested in the possibility that tighter regulation could improve Big Tech's financial performance in the near term. If hyperscalers respond by expanding internationally, the anticipated cash flow windfall could prove much smaller than expected. Wall Street appears to have found a silver lining following the Democrats' sweeping victories in the 2026 midterm elections. With Democrats gaining control of both chambers of Congress , investors are considering whether more regulation could slow the construction of artificial intelligence (AI) data centers across the United States. At first glance, that might actually benefit Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT), Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN), Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOGL) (NASDAQ: GOOG), and Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META). After all, building AI infrastructure is expensive. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » If Big Tech is forced to reduce capital expenditures (capex), their free cash flow could improve. Meanwhile, a shortage of compute capacity could allow existing data center operators to charge higher prices. While this all makes sense in theory, I think Wall Street may be overlooking an important possibility. Over the last several years, the hyperscalers have committed hundreds of billions of dollars to expanding AI infrastructure. These investments include procuring graphics processing units (GPUs), building data centers, and securing electricity. However, a number of candidates used data centers as a controversial topic during their time on the campaign trail. For many people around the country, data centers have fueled rising utility costs. Following the midterms, Wall Street is considering whether new legislation or tighter permitting requirements could make additional U.S. data center projects more difficult to pursue. The financial argument is pretty straightforward: If the hyperscalers slow down their infrastructure investments, capex would decline and free cash flow would rise. At the same time, continued demand for compute could create a supply demand imbalance. Companies with existing capacity would be in a position to charge higher utilization and command pricing power. The combination of lower spending and higher revenue per unit of compute would be favorable for the hyperscalers. With that said, this assumes that AI developers respond to potential regulatory restrictions by slowing down the pace of their infrastructure roadmaps. During a discussion with The Wall Street Journal on Nov. 4, Meta's president and vice chair, Dina Powell McCormick, acknowledged that the election results could complicate future data center development domestically. She says starting new domestic projects may be harder and raised a question that could reshape the AI investment narrative: "Do we need to build outside the United States?" There's already evidence that Big Tech is willing to invest internationally. Consider some of their existing projects: More than $10 billion is planned across the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Kuwait through 2030. More than $5 billion is planned in Mexico over 15 years. A $15 billion AI infrastructure investment planned for Visakhapatnam, India between 2026 and 2030. 13 billion Canadian dollars for a 1-gigawatt AI data center in Alberta, plus a 168-megawatt AI data center lease agreement in Jamnagar, India. Data source: Company press releases, Wall Street Journal , Reuters. These investments were announced before the midterms, so they shouldn't be interpreted as reactions to the election. Nevertheless, they demonstrate that hyperscalers already have international infrastructure strategies in place. If new restrictions make projects in certain states less attractive, I wouldn't be surprised to see Big Tech evaluate opportunities elsewhere and accelerate overseas development. Suppose new federal or state regulations delay data center construction in the U.S. Initially, the hyperscalers may postpone their projects, causing capex to decline and free cash flow to improve. In turn, investors may cheer these tighter cost controls and higher profits, leading to rising stock prices. Still, I question whether the hyperscalers would willingly delay expansion plans for two years while waiting for the 2028 presidential election. That strategy introduces another layer of uncertainty without guaranteeing a more favorable regulatory environment afterward. Most importantly, redirecting AI infrastructure investments overseas would not generate the sustained improvements to cash flow Wall Street is anticipating. The hyperscalers could easily continue pouring hundreds of billions of dollars annually on AI infrastructure, just in different countries. Ultimately, I think investors need to distinguish between a slowdown in U.S. data center construction and a slowdown in global AI investment. Those are two different outcomes. For now, Wall Street seems interested in the possibility that tighter regulation could improve Big Tech's financial performance in the near term. If hyperscalers respond by expanding internationally, the anticipated cash flow windfall could prove much smaller than expected. US midterm fallout and the stock market crash continue to weigh on the crypto market, as Bitcoin trades around $76,000. Yet three altcoins have shown unusual resilience. JUST (JST), Monero (XMR), and LEO Token (LEO) are holding important technical levels despite the broader market weakness. JUST trades near $0.1427, just below the $0.144 resistance that has repeatedly stopped its advance since October. The token has gained roughly 265% since February. Bullish: A daily close above $0.144 could trigger another upward move, particularly if trading volume increases. Bearish: Losing $0.135 would weaken the short-term setup. Deeper support sits near $0.114 and $0.104. Monero has fallen to around $612 from $623 yesterday. However, the privacy coin remains up more than 120% from its February low near $276. The bullish case rests on $600, a key Fibonacci level that previously acted as resistance. XMR recently reclaimed that level and has repeatedly tested it as support. Still, declining volume and a cooling RSI suggest buyers are losing some momentum. Bearish: A daily close below $600 would threaten the recovery, with $538 becoming the next major support. Bullish: Holding $600 and breaking 650–660 could open a move toward $688. LEO trades around $9.34, roughly 12% below its May all-time high of $10.61. Unlike most cryptocurrencies, it has barely moved during Bitcoin's latest decline. Since August, LEO has largely traded between $8.91 and $9.49. Buyers have repeatedly defended the lower boundary, while sellers have blocked attempts to break higher. However, thin trading volume makes its apparent stability less convincing. Bullish: Clearing 9.49–9.60 could push LEO toward $9.90, followed by its record high. For now, all three altcoins remain technically resilient. Their next moves will depend on whether buyers can defend support, particularly if Bitcoin breaks decisively below $75,000 again. US midterm fallout and the stock market crash continue to weigh on the crypto market, as Bitcoin trades around $76,000. Yet three altcoins have shown unusual resilience. JUST (JST), Monero (XMR), and LEO Token (LEO) are holding important technical levels despite the broader market weakness. JUST trades near $0.1427, just below the $0.144 resistance that has repeatedly stopped its advance since October. The token has gained roughly 265% since February. Bullish: A daily close above $0.144 could trigger another upward move, particularly if trading volume increases. Bearish: Losing $0.135 would weaken the short-term setup. Deeper support sits near $0.114 and $0.104. Monero has fallen to around $612 from $623 yesterday. However, the privacy coin remains up more than 120% from its February low near $276. The bullish case rests on $600, a key Fibonacci level that previously acted as resistance. XMR recently reclaimed that level and has repeatedly tested it as support. Still, declining volume and a cooling RSI suggest buyers are losing some momentum. Bearish: A daily close below $600 would threaten the recovery, with $538 becoming the next major support. Bullish: Holding $600 and breaking 650–660 could open a move toward $688. LEO trades around $9.34, roughly 12% below its May all-time high of $10.61. Unlike most cryptocurrencies, it has barely moved during Bitcoin's latest decline. Since August, LEO has largely traded between $8.91 and $9.49. Buyers have repeatedly defended the lower boundary, while sellers have blocked attempts to break higher. However, thin trading volume makes its apparent stability less convincing. Bullish: Clearing 9.49–9.60 could push LEO toward $9.90, followed by its record high. For now, all three altcoins remain technically resilient. Their next moves will depend on whether buyers can defend support, particularly if Bitcoin breaks decisively below $75,000 again. Investors betting on MARA (MARA) may be focused on the electric power the company controls at its own sites. You probably think of MARA as a bitcoin miner, but management now calls AI infrastructure the next use for those locations. Yet the stock fell 63.6% over the past year , while the S&P 500 returned 17.4%. So how much power is MARA putting together? MARA expects its power portfolio to reach about 4.8 gigawatts once pending deals close and receive necessary approvals. Management said on the fiscal Q2 2026 call that this expansion would more than double the company's current capacity. One of those deals is Long Ridge, a $1.5 billion acquisition by enterprise value . MARA is funding the purchase using bitcoin-backed debt and Long Ridge's own balance sheet rather than issuing new shares. The company has also bought the rights to a power site in Matagorda County, Texas, that could support about 2 gigawatts once it wins ERCOT and interconnection approval. Management expects the new capacity to let MARA move away from hosted mining, where other companies run its machines, as those agreements end by the first quarter of 2028. Why Does MARA's Power Matter While Bitcoin Falls? Investors fear a falling bitcoin price because MARA's sales still move with it. Revenue in fiscal Q2 2026 was $175 million, down 26.7% from a year earlier. A 28% drop in bitcoin prices weighed heavily on quarterly sales, but balance-sheet write-downs did the real damage: MARA posted a $3.46 billion net loss over the twelve months to June 30, 2026, largely dragged down by fair-value markdowns on its crypto stash. Long Ridge addresses part of that worry. Because long-term contracts cover about 70% of its output, that income appears to stand apart from the bitcoin price. MARA expects the deal to add about $144 million a year in EBITDA, its earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization. The price of Long Ridge equals about 30% of MARA's own enterprise value, which stood at $4.96 billion at the October 19, 2026 close. MARA's newer businesses remain small. Its blockchain finance platform has contract revenue, but management said that revenue will not be material to the company's total in the near term. Debt poses a risk for holders. MARA's total debt equals 87.6% of its market value, against 20.0% for the S&P 500. Long Ridge adds to that burden, since MARA expects to take on about $900 million of Long Ridge's debt, on top of $600 million in new borrowing. MARA has also pledged 54% of its bitcoin holdings as collateral for its borrowings. In the 2022 inflation shock, the stock fell 84.0%, against 24.0% for the S&P 500 ETF. MARA still needs approvals for the power plan. The Long Ridge deal will close only after FERC approves it, which management expects before year end. MARA also said it is working with Starwood on lease talks across several sites and is confident of signing at least two leases by then. The case for MARA rests on the power it is gathering, not the bitcoin it mines. FERC's ruling on Long Ridge and the first leases, both expected before the end of 2026, are the two things to watch. The company now sells much of its memory through customer contracts, however, and that may be what bears are missing.

extraction.body: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. Micron Technology (MU) stock fell 33.4% in the month to November 6, 2026, while the S&P 500 lost 4.9%. Bears argue that a memory maker’s profit follows chip prices, and Micron did run an operating loss in fiscal 2023. The company now sells much of its memory through customer contracts, however, and that may be what bears are missing. So how much of Micron’s fiscal 2027 output have its customers already committed to? Micron’s Customers Have Committed To Most Of Fiscal 2027 During its fiscal Q4 2026 earnings call on September 30, 2026, the company said customers have already committed to more than 75% of its fiscal 2027 shipments. This demand has allowed Micron to extend its chip allocation talks with customers out to 2028. Micron also holds agreements covering both DRAM and NAND that run through 2030 across every business unit, including the mobile and client business unit. These contracts also determine much of the pricing. A defined pricing framework covers about three quarters of the revenue under these agreements, while the remaining quarter is open to periodic negotiation or moves with the market. Most of these frameworks include floor and ceiling bands. As a result, Micron does not simply accept whatever the market pays each quarter for most of its contract revenue. Can Micron Keep Raising Prices Until New Supply Arrives? So far, yes, although management expects the increases to slow. Micron grew revenue on higher pricing and a better mix even in the mobile and client business unit, where bit shipments fell from the quarter before. During the same call, management said it expects margins to expand from the first quarter over the rest of fiscal 2027 on continued price increases “at a more moderate pace”. Management also expects market conditions to remain tight through 2028, while start-up costs will partly offset the gains from higher prices and a better mix. This matters because the bears’ worry has a real precedent. Micron’s revenue fell 49.5% from the year before in fiscal 2023, and the company posted an operating loss. The contracts do not eliminate the risk of new supply. Micron expects its Idaho facility to produce its first wafer output in mid-calendar 2027. Other chipmakers may open clean rooms as well, although meaningful supply growth takes a few quarters after that. Furthermore, the remaining fourth of contract revenue without a set framework can reprice through negotiation or the market, and the ceilings in most frameworks limit how much of a price increase Micron can keep. Micron trades at 9.2 times its trailing earnings , compared with 21.8 for the S&P 500. Those earnings came alongside a twelve-month operating margin of 74.6%, the highest of the 40 fiscal quarter ends since fiscal Q1 2017. Consequently, the low multiple rests on the best margins Micron has posted in ten years, not on an ordinary year. The stock has fallen further than the market in a broad sell-off. Micron stock fell 38% in the 2025 tariff shock , compared with 19% for the SPDR S&P 500 ETF. Customers have committed to most of Micron’s fiscal 2027 shipments, and the company is still raising prices, albeit more slowly by management’s own account. Of the two, the price increases are the less settled variable. Micron’s gross margin, which stood at 86.8% in fiscal Q4 2026, is the number to watch when the company reports fiscal Q1 2027 results in December 2026. How Much Micron Technology Do You Already Own? Investors betting on MARA (MARA) may be focused on the electric power the company controls at its own sites. You probably think of MARA as a bitcoin miner, but management now calls AI infrastructure the next use for those locations. Yet the stock fell 63.6% over the past year , while the S&P 500 returned 17.4%. So how much power is MARA putting together? MARA expects its power portfolio to reach about 4.8 gigawatts once pending deals close and receive necessary approvals. Management said on the fiscal Q2 2026 call that this expansion would more than double the company's current capacity. One of those deals is Long Ridge, a $1.5 billion acquisition by enterprise value . MARA is funding the purchase using bitcoin-backed debt and Long Ridge's own balance sheet rather than issuing new shares. The company has also bought the rights to a power site in Matagorda County, Texas, that could support about 2 gigawatts once it wins ERCOT and interconnection approval. Management expects the new capacity to let MARA move away from hosted mining, where other companies run its machines, as those agreements end by the first quarter of 2028. Why Does MARA's Power Matter While Bitcoin Falls? Investors fear a falling bitcoin price because MARA's sales still move with it. Revenue in fiscal Q2 2026 was $175 million, down 26.7% from a year earlier. A 28% drop in bitcoin prices weighed heavily on quarterly sales, but balance-sheet write-downs did the real damage: MARA posted a $3.46 billion net loss over the twelve months to June 30, 2026, largely dragged down by fair-value markdowns on its crypto stash. Long Ridge addresses part of that worry. Because long-term contracts cover about 70% of its output, that income appears to stand apart from the bitcoin price. MARA expects the deal to add about $144 million a year in EBITDA, its earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization. The price of Long Ridge equals about 30% of MARA's own enterprise value, which stood at $4.96 billion at the October 19, 2026 close. MARA's newer businesses remain small. Its blockchain finance platform has contract revenue, but management said that revenue will not be material to the company's total in the near term. Debt poses a risk for holders. MARA's total debt equals 87.6% of its market value, against 20.0% for the S&P 500. Long Ridge adds to that burden, since MARA expects to take on about $900 million of Long Ridge's debt, on top of $600 million in new borrowing. MARA has also pledged 54% of its bitcoin holdings as collateral for its borrowings. In the 2022 inflation shock, the stock fell 84.0%, against 24.0% for the S&P 500 ETF. MARA still needs approvals for the power plan. The Long Ridge deal will close only after FERC approves it, which management expects before year end. MARA also said it is working with Starwood on lease talks across several sites and is confident of signing at least two leases by then. The case for MARA rests on the power it is gathering, not the bitcoin it mines. FERC's ruling on Long Ridge and the first leases, both expected before the end of 2026, are the two things to watch. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox "The call from 1Q25 with Bitcoin above $100,000 was for it to lose a zero, on the back of a 20% drawdown in the S&P 500 (SPX) that stays down awhile, remains my base case," he wrote on X on Friday. A Bitcoin price that "loses a zero" would fall about 90%, to roughly $10,000. McGlone said that level carried the weight for the asset, noting that "10,000 Bitcoin is a key pivot." He also drew a link between crypto and stocks, saying that Bitcoin peaked on October 6 last year, while the Nasdaq peaked exactly a year later, on October 6, 2026. "May the market gods be with us all when we have the next stock bear market. I think it has started," he said. Bitcoin's price was trading at $75,830, up 0.2% during the past 24 hours, while the S&P 500 closed at 7,376 points on Friday, about 6% below its 52-week high of 7,844. That was well short of the 20% drop McGlone said would push Bitcoin toward $10,000. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around Bitcoin was in the 'bearish' zone, while chatter around it was at 'normal' levels over the past day. McGlone's post came in response to crypto trader and well-known investor Scott Melker, famously known as the "Wolf of All Streets." He said that the stock sell-off had not hit Bitcoin as hard as bears had expected. "Nasdaq entered correction territory today, more than 10% below its recent high," Melker said on X. Melker said the market had already covered half the drop that was meant to drag Bitcoin down. "The Nasdaq is down 10%, and we're still 17 or $18,000 above Bitcoin's low," he said. "The case that the Nasdaq or the market dropping 20% would send Bitcoin to $10,000, to me, or something way lower right now does not make any sense because we're halfway there." "The call from 1Q25 with Bitcoin above $100,000 was for it to lose a zero, on the back of a 20% drawdown in the S&P 500 (SPX) that stays down awhile, remains my base case," he wrote on X on Friday.
A Bitcoin price that "loses a zero" would fall about 90%, to roughly $10,000. McGlone said that level carried the weight for the asset, noting that "10,000 Bitcoin is a key pivot."
He also drew a link between crypto and stocks, saying that Bitcoin peaked on October 6 last year, while the Nasdaq peaked exactly a year later, on October 6, 2026.
"May the market gods be with us all when we have the next stock bear market. I think it has started," he said.

Bitcoin's price was trading at $75,830, up 0.2% during the past 24 hours, while the S&P 500 closed at 7,376 points on Friday, about 6% below its 52-week high of 7,844. That was well short of the 20% drop McGlone said would push Bitcoin toward $10,000.
On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around Bitcoin was in the 'bearish' zone, while chatter around it was at 'normal' levels over the past day.

McGlone's post came in response to crypto trader and well-known investor Scott Melker, famously known as the "Wolf of All Streets." He said that the stock sell-off had not hit Bitcoin as hard as bears had expected. "Nasdaq entered correction territory today, more than 10% below its recent high," Melker said on X.
Melker said the market had already covered half the drop that was meant to drag Bitcoin down. "The Nasdaq is down 10%, and we're still 17 or $18,000 above Bitcoin's low," he said.
"The case that the Nasdaq or the market dropping 20% would send Bitcoin to $10,000, to me, or something way lower right now does not make any sense because we're halfway there."

Van Eck saw no easy way out for Washington, and said, "We're going to inflate our way out of our debt." "There's no easy answer, and it's not going to be pretty." He also dismissed the idea that artificial intelligence (AI) would ease the pressure by pushing prices down. "All technology is deflationary," he said. He said it made sense because most financial advisers struggled to choose between tokens like Avalanche (AVAX) and Ethereum (ETH). "Most advisors can't pick Avalanche versus Ethereum or these kinds of things," he said. Van Eck saw no easy way out for Washington, and said, "We're going to inflate our way out of our debt." "There's no easy answer, and it's not going to be pretty." He also dismissed the idea that artificial intelligence (AI) would ease the pressure by pushing prices down. "All technology is deflationary," he said. "The foundational ones will survive, I think, and then the exchanges, I think, will survive," he said. sources.title: Binance Hackers Swap About $50 Million of Stolen XRP Mostly Into Bitcoin, Elliptic Says - Bitcoin Magazine
passages: Hackers tied to the record Binance theft have begun converting a large slice of the stolen XRP into bitcoin, blockchain analytics firm Elliptic said in an update dated through Friday, with about 42 million XRP — roughly $50 million — already swapped, mostly through THORChain.
Most early Tron laundering — about $220 million in TRX — has also run, a flow Bitcoin Magazine noted when covering the quiet shutdown of the T3 Financial Crime Unit before the hack.
Only small parts of the main ether and NEAR piles have moved.
Converted bitcoin from other stolen assets nearly doubled overnight to about 1,650 BTC, worth some $124 million, Elliptic wrote .

Since the Binance theft, Elliptic has counted more than 20,000 wallets on 16 blockchains, at least 36 services and at least 65,000 transactions — roughly one new wallet every 30 seconds and one transaction every 10 seconds.

The test now is whether THORChain operators and other bridges keep blocking the published attacker addresses fast enough to slow the XRP-to-bitcoin pipe, or whether the rest of that pile follows the same overnight path the first $50 million already took.
Some converted bitcoin has gone into Wasabi-style coinjoins — about 33 BTC, or $2.5 million, since Nov.

passages: WASHINGTON, Nov 7 (Reuters) - Environmental groups worldwide are using artificial intelligence to analyze climate data, track forest fires and count endangered wildlife – embracing a technology they also warn is driving a surge in electricity demand, water use and greenhouse-gas emissions.
But it would prefer to sidestep the technology due to its environmental impacts and is pushing back hard on the data center buildout.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres wants major AI companies to publicly disclose their systems' environmental impacts.

The World Resources Institute (WRI), a research group ​that uses AI to accelerate its climate and environmental analyses, said it limits resource-intensive applications such as generating videos and images, while caching AI query results ​so identical searches don't need to be reprocessed.
Some organizations are experimenting with ways to limit the environmental impact of their AI use.
Other groups now see AI as vital to effective environmental activism.

extraction.body: WASHINGTON, Nov 7 (Reuters) - Environmental groups worldwide are using artificial intelligence to analyze climate data, track forest fires and count endangered wildlife – embracing a technology they also warn is driving a surge in electricity demand, water use and greenhouse-gas emissions. The contradiction is forcing these organizations to justify their AI use in carrying out missions to combat climate change or protect natural resources. "We recognize that AI can come with environmental costs, and we ‌need to be thoughtful about how we use it," said Ali Swanson, AI lead at the US nonprofit Conservation International. "But at a time when the climate and biodiversity crises are becoming more urgent, AI can help us move faster and ‌make better use of the information we're collecting." The group recently started using AI to assess hotspots detected by satellites and send real-time alerts to community forest patrols about potential wildfires in remote and environmentally sensitive parts of Cambodia. Reuters interviewed 15 major environmental, conservation and development organizations about their AI use. All said they used the ​technology in some form and expressed concern about the environmental impact of the data centers powering it. The centers, filled with servers, can require vast amounts of electricity, along with water for cooling. It's a global dilemma for individuals, governments and industries balancing AI's benefits with its enormous risks. The tradeoffs likely will grab attention at the UN's COP31 climate conference this month, when host Turkey will call on governments, businesses and other institutions to sign a pledge outlining principles to ensure AI is developed and deployed sustainably. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres wants major AI companies to publicly disclose their systems' environmental impacts. Researchers at the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health estimate the global data-center footprint could more than double by 2030, reaching a size about twice that of Jakarta, the Indonesian megalopolis. The International Energy Agency, meanwhile, estimates global data centers will ‌consume about 945 terawatt-hours of electricity annually by 2030, producing the equivalent of more than 300 ⁠million metric tons of carbon dioxide. That's double current consumption and about equal to Japan's annual electricity use. The agency also projects that global data center water consumption will increase from about 560 billion liters (147.9 billion gallons) in 2023 to about 1.2 trillion liters (317 billion gallons) annually by 2030. sources.title: The Duo apps are coming, says Apple - TechCrunch
passages: The early iPhone Duo reviews were a bit hard on Apple’s new foldable for the lack of Duo-optimized apps available at the time of launch.
But Apple says things are changing quickly on the software front.

The Duo has also proven to be more popular than perhaps Apple had planned for, given its high price point. (It starts at $1,999 for the 256GB model.) The device quickly sold out within hours of orders opening up, and now, Duo ship times have shifted into the next year.
On its earnings call this week, Apple said it’s “hard to predict” when the Duo constraints leading to those delays will improve .
The company said that more than 2,000 app developers attended its over 50 in-person workshops that were hosted across 19 cities worldwide.

“It’s been wonderful to see how quickly developers have embraced iPhone Duo, and we’re grateful for their creativity and innovation,” said Susan Prescott, Apple’s vice president of Worldwide Developer Relations, in a statement referring to the 100,000-app milestone. “The enthusiasm has been incredible, and we’re excited to see the pace of updates continue to accelerate as more and more apps optimize for iPhone Duo,” she added.
Spotify, for instance, is still showing the black bar on the side, and the App Store doesn’t yet say an update is available on our review unit of the Duo.
However, given that this list comes directly from Apple, we expect to see these updates soon.

extraction.body: Some of the largest AI infrastructure projects in the world are underway in Texas. A dramatic political shift could slow their construction—and deepen concerns about the economics of the AI boom. Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech's largest AI buildouts. But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position. Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat against Ken Paxton. Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor against the Republican incumbent, Greg Abbott. At the state level, Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. Talarico and Hinojosa made data centers a central issue, discussing them constantly on the campaign trail. Even before the polls closed, insiders in the data center industry noticed that the times were changing. At the industry's DCD conference in Ashburn, Virginia, on Tuesday, panelists lamented that Texas had been the easiest place to build for years—until September. That's when Abbott, perhaps seeing the increasingly bipartisan distaste for these facilities , began changing course himself. Developers said the governor’s office had stopped responding to their emails. On September 21, Abbott directed a key state regulator to halt data center permits. Many panelists at the conference were expecting this to mean that existing projects might be slowed and new ones could be halted altogether. The governor-elect indeed seems eager to do that. Hinojosa supported tax breaks for data centers in 2023 as a way to boost construction jobs, but during her campaign she began pushing for a full-fledged moratorium. sources.title: Meta’s Muse AI can create custom ‘spaces’ for the version of the app you need right now
passages: Meta says you can create a new space by describing it.
Meta also announced that it’s bringing new “Active Memory” and “Active Focus” capabilities from its Muse Wonder AI model into the Muse app and its Meta AI chatbot.
Meta is rolling out spaces to all Muse users.
Meta will now allow you to build customized, app-like experiences within Muse.
“For example, keep your weekly planner up front during the workweek, then swap it for your weekend plans on Saturday,” Meta says.

If you connect an outside app to Muse — like Gmail, Google Calendar, OpenTable, Notion, and others Muse works with — the AI assistant will continuously pull information from them, allowing it to update pricing, dates, and other information in your space in the background.

sources.title: Ramp data shows AI spending stalling just as Anthropic nears its IPO
passages: A new report from Ramp shows AI spending flatlined over late summer even as token volumes rose, a sign that price competition and savvier customers may be capping revenue for OpenAI and Anthropic.
According to Ramp’s data, token spend only grew 1.5% across August and September.
To compare, in July, it grew 42% from the previous month.
Ramp data shows growth in spending among median and top 10%, but it’s not enough to make up the difference.
Median firms spend $12-$15 per employee per month, and the top 10% spend $600-$1,000.
In September, OpenAI cut API prices in half for GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna.

Answering the price war, Anthropic has also made significant reductions to pricing for Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 — a decision that the company said in a recent filing slashed revenue growth by about $600 million.
Both companies have also been offering enterprise discounts that are intended to lock-in spend, but in reality are hitting their revenue targets.
As Anthropic gears up for its IPO , the data suggests investors might be wrong to assume AI companies will keep growing at breakneck speed.
“Almost the entire spend on AI is from venture-backed, high-growth tech companies,” Ramp’s lead economist Ara Kharazian told TechCrunch.

“That’s fine as long as AI spend continues to rise, but if it starts to slow down because of something in the market or some other factor, they will all start to slow down simultaneously, and that could lead to other cascading effects.”
Bloomberg reported Friday that Anthropic’s potential valuation sank from the $2 trillion estimated in early October to just $1.2 to $1.3 trillion.
The company is also reportedly expected to receive a high “junk” rating from credit agencies.
OpenAI also lowered its proposed valuation to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion and slashed its latest fundraising goals by about $10 billion.
Much of the thesis for hypergrowth spending is that AI will undoubtedly introduce new use cases that will accelerate things.
AI coding emerged just a year and a half ago as the most commercially viable product that has led Anthropic and OpenAI to becoming trillion-dollar companies.
“Meta and Nvidia are also introducing enterprise offerings with pretty cheap models or open source models,” Kharazian said.
Kharazian says Ramp’s dataset likely informs many investor concerns.
There is, however, one potential brightside for spending trajectories, albeit a speculative one.
Notion co-founder Akshay Kothari recently posted internal data that matched Ramp’s insights.
As he succinctly put it: “tokens go brrr. costs go ahhh.”

extraction.body: Companies are using more AI than ever, but they’re not spending more on it. A new report from Ramp shows AI spending flatlined over late summer even as token volumes rose, a sign that price competition and savvier customers may be capping revenue for OpenAI and Anthropic. According to Ramp’s data, token spend only grew 1.5% across August and September. To compare, in July, it grew 42% from the previous month. As Anthropic gears up for its IPO , the data suggests investors might be wrong to assume AI companies will keep growing at breakneck speed. “Almost the entire spend on AI is from venture-backed, high-growth tech companies,” Ramp’s lead economist Ara Kharazian told TechCrunch. “That’s fine as long as AI spend continues to rise, but if it starts to slow down because of something in the market or some other factor, they will all start to slow down simultaneously, and that could lead to other cascading effects.” Kharazian said he’s already seeing evidence that the top 1% of firms — the most “ AI-pilled ” — have stuttered slightly in their spend in August and September, coming up just below the $10,000 per-employee they were hitting at their summer peaks. A slowdown among that cohort is “sufficient to slow down revenue entirely, despite the fact that we’re seeing rising volumes,” he said. Ramp data shows growth in spending among median and top 10%, but it’s not enough to make up the difference. Median firms spend $12-$15 per employee per month, and the top 10% spend $600-$1,000. “If you look at the use cases today, it’s not necessarily clear they will get up to that $10,000 per employee per month mark that the 1% is at,” Kharazian said. While there’s plenty of demand for AI coding agents in industries like software and finance, “it’s not necessarily true that a doctor’s office or a car dealership will need to spend that much on AI.” “The era of hypergrowth may be over, and now that we know there may not be as much juice to squeeze out of the top 1%,” he continued. October data did see a re-acceleration, with token spend up 8.9% from September 23 to October 23, but Kharazian said the headwinds on spend growth are strong. Kharazian (who has published a series of blogs called “ Cracks in the AI Thesis ”) said the slowdown isn’t due to a demand problem. Again, AI volumes are up. Instead he points to the competitive nature of the marketplace. “OpenAI and Anthropic price cuts have…just made it cheaper to use AI,” he said. In September, OpenAI cut API prices in half for GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna. Answering the price war, Anthropic has also made significant reductions to pricing for Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 — a decision that the company said in a recent filing slashed revenue growth by about $600 million. Both companies have also been offering enterprise discounts that are intended to lock-in spend, but in reality are hitting their revenue targets. Kharazian said this dynamic means it has very much become a buyer’s market. Subsidizing use of expensive technology in order to lock in customers has always been a part of the Big Tech playbook. Just recall how cheap it used to be to take an Uber or Lyft ride, and now that there are few other ride-hail players, the cost of going from A to B has risen significantly. Kharazian says those dynamics don’t work in the AI world because there’s just too much competition. “Meta and Nvidia are also introducing enterprise offerings with pretty cheap models or open source models,” Kharazian said. That’s partly due to the discounts from AI companies, but also because companies are just getting better at being thrifty. “As you get really advanced in using AI, you get better at figuring out how to control it,” Kharazian said. “You’re more likely to use defaults that prevent usage of very expensive models for long-running tasks. You’re more likely to impose some budgets on employees. You’re more likely to offload some of the spend from standard and light models to even cheaper light models via routers.” Notion co-founder Akshay Kothari recently posted internal data that matched Ramp’s insights. As Anthropic gears up for its IPO , the data suggests investors might be wrong to assume AI companies will keep growing at breakneck speed.

“Almost the entire spend on AI is from venture-backed, high-growth tech companies,” Ramp’s lead economist Ara Kharazian told TechCrunch. “That’s fine as long as AI spend continues to rise, but if it starts to slow down because of something in the market or some other factor, they will all start to slow down simultaneously, and that could lead to other cascading effects.”

Kharazian said he’s already seeing evidence that the top 1% of firms — the most “ AI-pilled ” — have stuttered slightly in their spend in August and September, coming up just below the $10,000 per-employee they were hitting at their summer peaks. A slowdown among that cohort is “sufficient to slow down revenue entirely, despite the fact that we’re seeing rising volumes,” he said.
Ramp data shows growth in spending among median and top 10%, but it’s not enough to make up the difference. Median firms spend $12-$15 per employee per month, and the top 10% spend $600-$1,000.

“If you look at the use cases today, it’s not necessarily clear they will get up to that $10,000 per employee per month mark that the 1% is at,” Kharazian said. While there’s plenty of demand for AI coding agents in industries like software and finance, “it’s not necessarily true that a doctor’s office or a car dealership will need to spend that much on AI.”
“The era of hypergrowth may be over, and now that we know there may not be as much juice to squeeze out of the top 1%,” he continued.
October data did see a re-acceleration, with token spend up 8.9% from September 23 to October 23, but Kharazian said the headwinds on spend growth are strong.

Kharazian (who has published a series of blogs called “ Cracks in the AI Thesis ”) said the slowdown isn’t due to a demand problem. Again, AI volumes are up. Instead he points to the competitive nature of the marketplace.

“OpenAI and Anthropic price cuts have…just made it cheaper to use AI,” he said. In September, OpenAI cut API prices in half for GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna. Answering the price war, Anthropic has also made significant reductions to pricing for Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 — a decision that the company said in a recent filing slashed revenue growth by about $600 million. Both companies have also been offering enterprise discounts that are intended to lock-in spend, but in reality are hitting their revenue targets.
Kharazian said this dynamic means it has very much become a buyer’s market.

Subsidizing use of expensive technology in order to lock in customers has always been a part of the Big Tech playbook. Just recall how cheap it used to be to take an Uber or Lyft ride, and now that there are few other ride-hail players, the cost of going from A to B has risen significantly. Kharazian says those dynamics don’t work in the AI world because there’s just too much competition.

“Meta and Nvidia are also introducing enterprise offerings with pretty cheap models or open source models,” Kharazian said. He also pointed to the range of other open model companies from China and the United States, as well as a new company called Jev — a lightweight tool for choosing between a few predetermined outputs — that is increasingly among the top performers on Ramp.
“For a lot of AI use cases, you just need a simple Yes/No,” Kharazian said. “So you take your already cheap models, you shift them over to Jev, and now your already cheap stuff gets even cheaper.”

The ability to complete workloads at a much cheaper cost is another factor driving the spending slowdown. That’s partly due to the discounts from AI companies, but also because companies are just getting better at being thrifty.

“As you get really advanced in using AI, you get better at figuring out how to control it,” Kharazian said. “You’re more likely to use defaults that prevent usage of very expensive models for long-running tasks. You’re more likely to impose some budgets on employees. You’re more likely to offload some of the spend from standard and light models to even cheaper light models via routers.”
Notion co-founder Akshay Kothari recently posted internal data that matched Ramp’s insights. As he succinctly put it: “tokens go brrr. costs go ahhh.”

“A lot of the assumptions that we had about the trajectory of AI spend are starting to break down,” Kharazian said. “You can use more AI, but use it for less. That’s great for the customers…but it’s not necessarily great for the model companies. And it does introduce new questions around their revenue trajectories.”

Bloomberg reported Friday that Anthropic’s potential valuation sank from the $2 trillion estimated in early October to just $1.2 to $1.3 trillion. The company is also reportedly expected to receive a high “junk” rating from credit agencies. OpenAI also lowered its proposed valuation to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion and slashed its latest fundraising goals by about $10 billion.
Kharazian says Ramp’s dataset likely informs many investor concerns. There is, however, one potential brightside for spending trajectories, albeit a speculative one.

Much of the thesis for hypergrowth spending is that AI will undoubtedly introduce new use cases that will accelerate things. AI coding emerged just a year and a half ago as the most commercially viable product that has led Anthropic and OpenAI to becoming trillion-dollar companies. The hope among investors is that there will be another revolution that will drive further spend.

Some think personal agents will be the next coding agents. OpenAI , SpaceXAI , and Meta have all released their own personal agents, alongside startups like Instinct . Kharazian is skeptical, though, that personal agents, which are “not as economically productive as coding,” will provide the boost the industry needs for nonstop growth.

“The projection is that there will be new products being introduced that will drive further growth,” Kharazian said. “But based on what we can observe today and the products available and what is commercially advanced, AI spend has started to slow down.”
